title: Act I, Scene IV

teacherSummary.text: Masked and carrying torches, Romeo, Mercutio and Benvolio head to the Capulet feast. Romeo, heavy-hearted, says he dreamed a dream; Mercutio answers with the Queen Mab speech about a fairy who drives through sleepers' brains and gives them dreams, ending in darker images. Romeo fears a consequence 'hanging in the stars' will begin tonight, but goes on.

criticalVoices.quote: Wit ever wakeful, fancy busy and procreative as an insect, courage, an easy mind that, without cares of its own, is at once disposed to laugh away those of others, and yet to be interested in them,--these and all congenial qualities, melting into the common 'copula' of them all, the man of rank and the gentleman, with all its excellencies and all its weaknesses, constitute the character of Mercutio!
criticalVoices.speaker: Samuel Taylor Coleridge, poet and critic
criticalVoices.source: Notes on Romeo and Juliet, in The Literary Remains of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Vol. 2 (1836), note on Act I, Scene iv
criticalVoices.useNote: Character web: match each trait in Coleridge's list to a line from Queen Mab.
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Analyze Mercutio's Queen Mab speech and character.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Romeo enters the Capulet house expecting disaster but chooses to go on. Useful evidence: “O, then, I see Queen Mab hath been with you” (Act I, Scene IV, Mercutio (speech 23)): Mercutio mocks dreams as the work of a fairy. On imagery: Mab drives "Athwart men's noses as they lie asleep": tiny, precise images that grow darker. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
